intro: Frank Lévy plays Chopin’s Ballade No. 1 in G minor, Op. 23, which opens Largo before the Moderato. Its G minor melody and E♭ major second theme both return later at greater force, and the work ends with a coda marked Presto con fuoco, very fast, with fire.

sections.label: Intro · Largo, octaves rising from the bass
sections.mNote: Both hands rise in octaves and stop on a dissonance.

sections.label: A · G minor theme, Moderato
sections.mNote: A circling melody over detached bass notes and chords.

sections.label: B · Melody in E♭ major
sections.mNote: A broad melody above rolling left-hand chords.

sections.label: Dev · A minor turns to A major
sections.mNote: The first theme returns; the second follows in full chords.

sections.label: B′ · E♭ major melody in full chords
sections.mNote: The E♭ major melody returns fortissimo over broken chords.

sections.label: A′ · G minor over a low D
sections.mNote: The first theme returns above repeated bass notes.

sections.label: Coda · Presto con fuoco
sections.mNote: Leaping chords and displaced accents in the fast ending.

sections.label: C · Scales and chords in G minor
sections.mNote: Runs cross the keyboard between heavy G minor chords.

cues.title: Opening in octaves, Largo
cues.text: The marking is Largo. Both hands start on C and climb an octave apart, outlining A♭ major. The line reaches the treble, pauses and moves into chords, with an E♭ sounding against the D below it.
cues.evidence: Chopin, Ballade Op. 23, Klindworth edition (Bote & Bock, c. 1880), bars 1–7. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=1959
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: First theme, Moderato
cues.text: The piano moves into Moderato and a six-beat bar. A circling melody in G minor lies above detached bass notes and chords, with the accompaniment in the left hand.
cues.evidence: Klindworth edition, bars 8–16: 6/4, Moderato, and the first theme’s detached left-hand accompaniment.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Second theme in E♭ major
cues.text: The second theme opens in E♭ major, marked meno mosso (less movement). The right hand plays long notes above rolling chords in the left hand, and the phrase extends over several bars.
cues.evidence: Klindworth edition, pickup in bar 67 and theme in bars 68–81; E♭ major and meno mosso.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Return of the first theme, A minor
cues.text: The first melody returns in A minor at bar 94. Low repeated Es replace the opening accompaniment. The second theme follows in A major at bar 107.
cues.evidence: Klindworth edition, bars 94–106: first-theme return over repeated E; A-major second theme at bar 107.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Second theme in A major
cues.text: The second theme returns in A major, with full chords in the right hand and a low A in the bass. Where it was first heard over a light accompaniment, it now spans both ends of the keyboard.
cues.evidence: Klindworth edition, bars 106–113: E dominant harmony resolves to A major; chordal second theme above left-hand arpeggios.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Schumann and Chopin, Leipzig, 1836
cues.text: In Leipzig in 1836 Schumann told Chopin that this Ballade was his favourite of Chopin’s works. According to Schumann, Chopin paused for a long time before he replied: “I’m glad of that because it’s the one I prefer too.”
cues.evidence: Schumann’s account of the 1836 Leipzig meeting, quoted by Orrin Howard in the LA Phil programme note. https://www.laphil.com/works/ballade-no-1-in-g-minor-op-23

cues.title: Return of the second theme, E♭ major
cues.text: The second theme returns first, in its original E♭ major. Chopin marks it fortissimo, with broken chords in the left hand throughout. The melody keeps its long notes.
cues.evidence: Klindworth edition, bars 166–179: fortissimo return of the second theme, with continuous left-hand broken chords.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Return of the first theme
cues.text: The first theme returns in G minor, marked meno mosso, while the left hand repeats a low D. The return is short. D major chords build up under it, preparing the coda.
cues.evidence: Klindworth edition, bars 194–207: quiet first-theme return, repeated D bass and dominant preparation.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Coda, Presto con fuoco
cues.text: The coda, marked Presto con fuoco, starts with a low G and leaping chords. In bars 208–215 the metre changes from 6/4 to 4/4. Accents fall inside the bar, and the right hand repeatedly drops from a high chord to a single lower note.
cues.evidence: Klindworth edition, bars 208–215: Presto con fuoco, change from 6/4 to 4/4, low G and displaced right-hand chord accents.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Closing bars in G minor
cues.text: Over a sustained low G, scales rise up the keyboard. G minor chords break off the runs, and rests break off the chords. The last descent is in chromatic octaves, ending on G.
cues.evidence: Klindworth edition, bars 250–264: sustained bass G, ascending scales, interrupted chordal passages and chromatic octaves.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

transitions.title: From Largo octaves to quiet melody
transitions.from: Intro · Largo, octaves rising from the bass
transitions.how: The Largo ends with E♭ above a bass D. At Moderato the metre changes to 6/4 and the hands separate into melody and accompaniment. A low D introduces the quiet G minor theme, and detached bass notes and chords follow.

transitions.title: Running figures stop before E♭ major
transitions.how: The running figures thin out and stop. Under meno mosso, the right hand begins a long phrase in E♭ major, and the left hand plays broken chords beneath it. The six-beat bar continues, and the melody spans it.
transitions.evidence: Klindworth edition, bars 62–75: smorzando, rests, meno mosso and E♭-major second theme.

transitions.title: First theme returns in A minor
transitions.to: Dev · A minor turns to A major
transitions.how: The E♭ major melody slows through its last decorated phrases. Repeated low Es then sound beneath the first theme, now in A minor (bars 90–107 in the Klindworth edition). The accompaniment starts thinly and thickens into E dominant chords, which lead to the second theme in A major.
transitions.evidence: Klindworth edition, bars 90–107: first-theme return in A minor over E, followed by E dominant harmony and A major.

transitions.title: Descending run to the second theme
transitions.from: Dev · A minor turns to A major
transitions.to: B′ · E♭ major melody in full chords
transitions.how: A long descending run reaches B♭ in the bass. The lyrical theme returns above it in full chords, fortissimo, and the bass moves to E♭. Beneath the melody the left hand continues in broken chords.
transitions.evidence: Klindworth edition, bars 164–169: descending run, B♭ bass at bar 166, E♭ at bar 167 and chordal second-theme return.

transitions.title: First theme returns over D
transitions.from: B′ · E♭ major melody in full chords
transitions.to: A′ · G minor over a low D
transitions.how: The right-hand runs slow down and fall towards the middle of the piano. At meno mosso, the first theme returns in G minor above repeated low Ds, marked pianissimo, in place of the broad E♭ major melody. In the Klindworth edition this join falls in bars 188–199, with a rallentando before the meno mosso.
transitions.evidence: Klindworth edition, bars 188–199: rallentando, meno mosso and repeated D bass under the first theme.

transitions.title: From D major dominant to the coda
transitions.from: A′ · G minor over a low D
transitions.how: The right hand descends over dominant harmony on D. The coda begins on a low G, marked Presto con fuoco, and the metre changes from 6/4 to 4/4. In the right hand, high chords leap down to single notes. The left hand alternates bass notes and chords.
transitions.evidence: Klindworth edition, bars 206–211: D dominant harmony, low G and the change from 6/4 to 4/4 at the coda.

composer.born: 1 March 1810, Żelazowa Wola, Duchy of Warsaw
composer.epithet: Composer for the piano, known for music that drew on operatic singing and on the irregular accents of the mazurka.
facts: Wojciech Żywny; composition with Józef Elsner in Warsaw, 1826–29
Warsaw · Paris from 1831 · summers at Nohant
Piano lessons, publishing and occasional concerts
The piano, from a few lines of mazurka to concertos and sonatas
composer.background:
In February 1832 Chopin, a twenty-one-year-old Polish pianist, played in the Pleyel rooms in Paris. He had arrived the previous autumn, with two concertos behind him. The concert caught the attention of the city’s publishers, and teaching soon supplied his living. For the rest of his life his profession depended on people hearing him at close quarters. The great public virtuosos travelled from one concert city to the next; Chopin stayed in Paris and gave lessons.

He was born at Żelazowa Wola in 1810. His father, Nicolas, had come from France and worked as a tutor; his mother, Justyna Krzyżanowska, was Polish. The family moved to Warsaw while Fryderyk was still a baby, when Nicolas obtained a teaching post at the Lyceum. At seven the boy had a polonaise in print. Wojciech Żywny taught him the piano, with Bach and Mozart among his models; Józef Elsner later gave him a rigorous training in composition at Warsaw’s Main School of Music.
